newsitem.title: USA: US hog prices dip seasonally but extent questioned.
newsitem.headline: US hog prices dip seasonally but extent questioned.

text.p: U.S. Midwest cash hog prices started their seasonal slide last week, but livestock analysts questioned whether prices will follow the 10-year average break of $10.00 per hundredweight (cwt) from the summer peak.

Interior Iowa/southern Minnesota cash hog prices in direct sales averaged $59.43 per cwt in July and could average from $58.00 to $59.00 in August, said Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst with Alaron Trading Corp. in Chicago.
A normal seasonal break of $10.00 would put the hog price near the high $40.00-level by November, he said.
"How much of a size of the break really relates to how much production is going to be down relative to last year in the final quarter (Oct-Dec)," Levitt said.

Right now the market is not sure if production is going to be down three percent or six percent, so the market is hanging around $53.00-$54.00 as far as hog futures against the October and December contracts are concerned, he said.
At Monday's close, hog futures on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange closed at 54.650 cents a lb on hogs for delivery against October futures and 54.525 cents on hogs for December.
The U.S. Agriculture Department in June said the number of pigs born in the March-May period were down six percent from a year ago.
If pork production in the final quarter of 1996 is in turn, down six percent, the market can maintain a $54.00 or $55.00 price average for the final quarter, Levitt said.

"If it's down only three percent, it suggests a $50.00-$52.00 price and if it's down more than six percent, like eight or nine percent, then the chances are, we may not get very much of a cash break at all, " Levitt said.
The number of hogs for slaughter is picking up in absolute terms relative to June and July, which accounts for the seasonal slide that started last week, he said.

Weekly slaughter has steadily expanded from 1.592 million head the week ended July 27th to 1.761 million last week. Monday's hog slaughter was estimated at 335,000 head, up 15,000 from a week ago, according to USDA.

"Last week, hog numbers increased 31,000 head and prices fell $1.00-$2.00 to $58.00, with a few at $58.50. If we kill 1.8 million head this week, then the chances are, we can take another dollar or so, off the market," Levitt said.
Hog prices in September likely will be about $54.00 to $55.00 if kills don't get much above 1.8 million head but if they go above 1.9 million, they will probably head to $52, Levitt said.
But hog prices could be underpinned by consistent demand and tight supplies of frozen pork, particularly hams, said Dale Benson, Chicago-based analyst with Dean-Witter Reynolds.

Frozen pork stocks on July 31 totaled 321.537 million lbs, down 8.6 percent from June and down 21.3 percent from a year ago, according to USDA. Bone-in ham stocks were pegged at 50.368 million lbs, down 5.1 percent from a month ago and down 39.5 percent from a year ago.
"We had packers chasing hogs early this summer for belly supplies and they will continue to chase them in the fall for ham stocks," Benson said.
Demand for hogs will be more pronounced in November and early December as demand for holiday hams rises, Benson said.
But, even that support could be offset by the marketing of more hogs at heavier weights than a year ago because the animals have not been stressed by hot weather this summer.

The average weight of barrows and gilts in Iowa-Southern Minnesota for the week ended August 17 was 245.4 lbs, 0.7 lbs heavier than the previous week and 2.2 lbs heavier than a year ago, according to USDA.
